c12_hs_ch09.subtitle: The number was right — the food matrix was missing
c12_hs_ch09.intro: One family, four plates, four different RDAs — a pregnant mother, an infant, a labourer, an elder.
c12_hs_ch09.goal: Use RDA correctly — requirements shift with age, sex, activity and physiology; food beats the isolated pill.

discovery.question: Dal, roti, potato sabzi at lunch — then roti, dal, potato sabzi again at dinner. The family's fed, so what's wrong with this menu?
options: It fails three principles at once — no variety (potato twice), no fruit or milk group, and no moderation in the oil; feeding people isn't the same as planning meals
Nothing — it's healthy food
Potato is a vegetable
Indians eat this daily
discovery.answer: It fails three principles at once — no variety (potato twice), no fruit or milk group, and no moderation in the oil; feeding people isn't the same as planning meals
discovery.hook: Variety isn't decoration — nutritionally, no single food carries every nutrient; psychologically, monotony kills appetite, especially in children and elders. And the food pyramid is a starting grid, not a guarantee: it speaks to a reference adult, not your anaemic mother or hypertensive father.

c12_hs_ch10.mission: Plan a real family week: run balance, variety, moderation, adequacy and economy across four different bodies, and catch the violations hiding in an ordinary thali.
c12_hs_ch10.finale: You can now plan meals as nutrient architecture — and hear the difference between feeding people and nourishing them.
c12_hs_ch10.subtitle: Same potato twice — three principles broken
c12_hs_ch10.intro: Four people, four different needs, one kitchen — meal planning is the framework that turns science into plates.
c12_hs_ch10.goal: Apply the five principles of meal planning — balance, variety, moderation, adequacy, economy — to real Indian menus.

discovery.question: A mother's nursing degree and a family's car are both 'resources' — but which can the family actually share, and which lives only in one person?
options: The skill is individual, the car shared — the qualification stays in her body though its salary becomes family money; the resource and its output aren't the same thing
Both are shared
The car is individual
Degrees transfer
discovery.answer: The skill is individual, the car shared — the qualification stays in her body though its salary becomes family money; the resource and its output aren't the same thing
discovery.hook: Resources aren't just money and time — skills, energy, a community park all count. Interchangeable doesn't mean manageable: a park substitutes for a garden but nobody controls its hours; money can buy time, but time can't store itself.

c12_hs_ch11.mission: Map a household's true wealth: classify resources across human/non-human and individual/shared/natural/community, then run a 20% electricity cut through all five management steps.
c12_hs_ch11.finale: You can now inventory a family's real assets — and see why the scarcest resource is often the one nobody counted.
c12_hs_ch11.subtitle: Her degree is hers; the salary is the family's
c12_hs_ch11.intro: A family's real wealth isn't in the bank — it's in skills, time, energy and shared things nobody itemised.
c12_hs_ch11.goal: Classify family resources and run the five-step management cycle on a concrete household goal.

discovery.question: A worker lectures thirty mothers on breastfeeding with slides; they listen silently and leave. Information delivered — so why isn't this extension education?
options: It violated the philosophy — teacher-centred, expert-agenda, no participation; extension starts where the people are, not where the PowerPoint begins
The topic was wrong
Mothers were tired
No projector budget
discovery.answer: It violated the philosophy — teacher-centred, expert-agenda, no participation; extension starts where the people are, not where the PowerPoint begins
discovery.hook: Extension's scope isn't just agriculture — it spans health, home science and community development as one participatory weave. And the real test is behaviour change and self-reliance, not awareness: a lecture measured by attendance is formal education in a field.

c12_hs_ch12.mission: Build an anaemia programme the extension way: needs assessment with the girls themselves, map local iron-rich foods, facilitate recipe trials — and spot why 'give tablets and lecture' misses the point.
c12_hs_ch12.finale: You can now tell education for life from education in a classroom — where the learner is partner, not audience.
c12_hs_ch12.subtitle: A lecture that changed nothing — and why
c12_hs_ch12.intro: The village sells its nutritious crops and buys polished rice. Extension begins by asking why — not by telling.
c12_hs_ch12.goal: Distinguish extension's participatory, problem-solving philosophy from formal education's classroom model.

discovery.question: A hospital buys an MRI; a distributor buys the same MRI to resell. Two organisations, one machine — only one is a 'consumer' under the law. Which, and why?
options: The hospital — consumer status follows end-use, not buyer type; the distributor purchases for resale, which the Act excludes
The distributor — whoever pays for goods counts as a consumer
Both — the Act protects every purchase of goods or services equally
Neither — consumer status applies only to individuals, never organisations
discovery.answer: The hospital — consumer status follows end-use, not buyer type; the distributor purchases for resale, which the Act excludes
discovery.hook: 'Anyone who pays is a consumer' is wrong — the law protects personal, household and self-employment purchases only. A freelancer's laptop is a consumer purchase; a factory's raw cotton is not. Purpose, not payment, is the test.

c12_hs_ch13.mission: Run the purpose test on edge cases: the farmer's own tractor versus the contractor's rental fleet, the school's mid-day meal versus the corporation's bridge steel — and draft a lawyer's three-question checklist.
c12_hs_ch13.finale: You can now define 'consumer' the way the law does — by what the purchase is FOR, not who paid for it.
c12_hs_ch13.subtitle: Same machine, different buyer — the law sees the purpose
c12_hs_ch13.intro: Three shoppers buy the same notebooks — mother, principal, kirana owner. Only two are consumers.
c12_hs_ch13.goal: Classify consumers by purpose of purchase — and why resellers fall outside the Act's protection.

discovery.question: The same turmeric-dal spill stains cotton deep and rinses off polyester. What makes one fibre hold the soil and the other shrug it off?
options: Structure — cotton's hydrophilic, amorphous regions pull water-borne soil in by capillary action; polyester's crystalline hydrophobic surface keeps it on top
Cotton is cheaper
Polyester is coated
Turmeric loves cotton
discovery.answer: Structure — cotton's hydrophilic, amorphous regions pull water-borne soil in by capillary action; polyester's crystalline hydrophobic surface keeps it on top
discovery.hook: Washing isn't always rescue — hot alkaline water felts wool, chlorine bleach tenders cotton; laundering is controlled deterioration. And soil and decay team up: embedded grit abrades fibres like sandpaper while sweat's acids hydrolyse silk.

c12_hs_ch14.mission: Read a stain like a chemist: classify soils by their nature, predict which fibre suffers most, and judge when the wash itself is the damage.
c12_hs_ch14.finale: You can now see fabric care as materials science — where the wrong wash destroys faster than the dirt ever could.
c12_hs_ch14.subtitle: The spill was equal — the fibre decided
c12_hs_ch14.intro: Why does one kurta stain for good and the other rinse clean? The answer is written in the fibre's chemistry.
c12_hs_ch14.goal: Link fibre structure to soiling and deterioration — and why washing can be the damage, not the cure.

discovery.question: A canteen balance stored as FLOAT quietly drifts paise across a thousand transactions — ₹12345.67 becomes 12345.6700000001. What should the column have been?
options: DECIMAL(10,2) — fixed-point stores money exactly; FLOAT's binary approximation accumulates errors that audits will find
DOUBLE — more precision
INT — store paise
VARCHAR — store text
discovery.answer: DECIMAL(10,2) — fixed-point stores money exactly; FLOAT's binary approximation accumulates errors that audits will find
discovery.hook: 'VARCHAR always saves space' fails on a 10-digit mobile — the length-prefix byte makes it bigger than CHAR(10). And a PIN code isn't a number: leading zeros matter, and nobody sums PINs. The smallest safe type is a design decision, not a default.

c12_ip_ch01.mission: Design a schema that respects reality: pick types for balance, recharge date, status code and notes; weigh TIMESTAMP's 1970 floor against DATETIME's reach; and defend CHAR for data that never varies.
c12_ip_ch01.finale: You can now choose data types by constraint, not habit — and catch the penny-sized errors that compound into audit findings.
c12_ip_ch01.subtitle: FLOAT lost the paise — DECIMAL keeps them honest
c12_ip_ch01.intro: Every column type is a promise about what values are legal — and what the storage bill will be.
c12_ip_ch01.goal: Choose MySQL data types by range, precision and storage — money exact, dates ranged, strings honest.

discovery.question: You hand pandas a dictionary of monthly sales — and the months become the index without being asked. Where did the labels come from?
options: The keys — a dict's keys become the Series index in insertion order, values become data; no index argument means pandas builds 0,1,2... only when nothing else provides labels
The values did
Alphabetical order
Random order
discovery.answer: The keys — a dict's keys become the Series index in insertion order, values become data; no index argument means pandas builds 0,1,2... only when nothing else provides labels
discovery.hook: List or NumPy array — same default RangeIndex; the source container doesn't matter. And 'sales[1]' works but 'sales['Feb']' is the point: labels are addresses you chose, not positions you memorised.

c12_ip_ch02.mission: Build Series three ways — list, array, dict — predict each index before printing, and catch the case where a custom index asks for a label the data never had.
c12_ip_ch02.finale: You can now read a Series as labelled data — where the index is an address book, not a row number.
c12_ip_ch02.subtitle: The dictionary's keys became the address book
c12_ip_ch02.intro: A week's temperatures become answerable questions the moment each value gets a label.
c12_ip_ch02.goal: Create Pandas Series from lists, arrays and dicts — and predict the index each way.

discovery.question: Two laptops joined by one Ethernet cable — is that a network? Not until something invisible agrees to the conversation. What's missing?
options: Protocols and configuration — addressing, TCP/IP, sharing services; the cable is only the medium, the rules make it a network
A faster cable — two nodes need real bandwidth before they can exchange data
Internet access — a link is not a network until it can reach the web
A shared password — security credentials are what authorise the connection
discovery.answer: Protocols and configuration — addressing, TCP/IP, sharing services; the cable is only the medium, the rules make it a network
discovery.hook: A network is defined by function, not wires — one printer serving thirty PCs is the purpose made visible. And 'network' vs 'distributed system' is the transparency line: in a network you know there are many machines; a distributed system hides them behind one face.

c12_ip_ch03.mission: Wire a school lab for sharing: list the hardware AND the protocol layer that makes one printer serve thirty machines, then weigh connection against purpose.
c12_ip_ch03.finale: You can now define a network by what it enables — and spot the protocol layer invisible inside every 'connected' device.
c12_ip_ch03.subtitle: The cable was hardware — the protocols made it a network
c12_ip_ch03.intro: Fifty computers, one printer, one internet line — the network is the agreement that lets them share.
c12_ip_ch03.goal: Define a network by function — nodes, links, protocols, and resource sharing over mere connection.

discovery.question: A student who posts nothing insists she has no digital footprint — yet phone ads for a product she searched once follow her for weeks. What is she missing?
options: Passive traces — ISP logs, cookies, device fingerprints and metadata record her without a single post; the footprint isn't what you publish, it's what the network keeps
Incognito deletes it
No posts, no data
Ads are coincidence
discovery.answer: Passive traces — ISP logs, cookies, device fingerprints and metadata record her without a single post; the footprint isn't what you publish, it's what the network keeps
discovery.hook: Deleting an account doesn't erase the trail — brokers already scraped it into shadow profiles, and platforms retain logs and 'anonymised' analytics beyond the delete button. One UPI order leaves active data you typed and passive data you never saw — the payment record outlives the GPS ping by years.

c12_ip_ch04.mission: Audit a single online order: separate active footprints from passive ones, rank which records persist longest, and design an audit checklist for the footprints you forgot you made.
c12_ip_ch04.finale: You can now see the internet's other ledger — the one recording you whether or not you ever post.
c12_ip_ch04.subtitle: She never posted — and the internet still knows
c12_ip_ch04.intro: Footprints on wet sand wash away; digital ones get copied, sold and aggregated. Learn to see your own trail.
c12_ip_ch04.goal: Distinguish active from passive digital footprints — and why deletion never fully erases them.

discovery.question: WhatsApp runs on the internet but never touches the web — while YouTube needs both. What's the actual dividing line?
options: The internet is the infrastructure; the web is one service riding on it — email, VoIP and WhatsApp are internet services that aren't the web
Same thing, two names
Web is bigger
Apps vs browsers only
discovery.answer: The internet is the infrastructure; the web is one service riding on it — email, VoIP and WhatsApp are internet services that aren't the web
discovery.hook: Three pillars built the web — URL locates, HTML structures, HTTP transfers — and they came decades after the internet existed. 'Checking email in a browser' doesn't make email a web service; the access method isn't the service.

c12_ip_ch05.mission: Split the two layers cleanly: assign everyday services to internet-or-web, map the three pillars' jobs, and weigh the claim that the web made the internet public.
c12_ip_ch05.finale: You can now separate the road from the traffic — and explain why the web is a passenger, not the highway.
c12_ip_ch05.subtitle: The internet is the road; the web is one kind of traffic
c12_ip_ch05.intro: Two words everyone uses interchangeably — and a distinction every web page silently depends on.
c12_ip_ch05.goal: Distinguish the internet from the web — and the roles of URL, HTML and HTTP.

discovery.question: A student writes a heading inside the head tag and wonders why it never renders — the browser obeyed perfectly. What's the head actually for?
options: Invisible instructions — metadata like charset, viewport and title that steer the browser but never paint the page; visible content lives in body
Page headers — the head tag is where top-of-page titles belong
Styling only — head exists to hold CSS links and fonts
SEO tags only — search engines read it but browsers ignore it entirely
discovery.answer: Invisible instructions — metadata like charset, viewport and title that steer the browser but never paint the page; visible content lives in body
discovery.hook: The doctype isn't a tag — it's a mode switch telling the browser 'standards, not quirks.' And head versus body isn't optional decoration: it's the contract between your code and the rendering engine.

c12_ip_ch06.mission: Write the five-line skeleton from memory: doctype, html, head, body — then place charset, viewport and title correctly and explain what each one quietly controls.
c12_ip_ch06.finale: You can now build a valid HTML5 skeleton — and know which tags speak to the browser instead of the reader.
c12_ip_ch06.subtitle: The heading in <head> rendered nothing — correctly
c12_ip_ch06.intro: Before a single visible word, every page negotiates with the browser through tags nobody sees.
c12_ip_ch06.goal: Structure a valid HTML5 document — doctype, head metadata, body content — and know what each part controls.

discovery.question: 'I have no money and post nothing secret — cyber safety isn't for me.' What three threats does this teenager still carry?
options: Identity theft on her Aadhaar, a phone turned botnet, and private data harvested for sextortion — none need a bank balance
Only money matters
Antivirus covers it
Teens aren't targets
discovery.answer: Identity theft on her Aadhaar, a phone turned botnet, and private data harvested for sextortion — none need a bank balance
discovery.hook: 'Scan the attachment with antivirus first' is already too late — verify the sender domain, distrust urgency, cross-check on the official site. And café Wi-Fi versus weak home Wi-Fi aren't equal threats: sniffing thrives on public networks, but liability lands on the home subscriber.

c12_ip_ch07.mission: Run the decision framework on a fake CBSE admit-card email: verify domain, refuse urgency, never open the attachment — then weigh which individual moves defeat even sophisticated attacks.
c12_ip_ch07.finale: You can now treat cyber safety as a daily decision framework — where 2FA, zero-trust verification and offline backups beat learned helplessness.
c12_ip_ch07.subtitle: No money, no secrets — still a target
c12_ip_ch07.intro: A WhatsApp 'KYC expired' link is the exam question you answer in real life. Learn the framework before you click.
c12_ip_ch07.goal: Adopt cyber safety as personal defence — risk categories, verification discipline and individual countermeasures.

discovery.question: Group students by birth month for relay teams — is that a fair mathematical grouping? What three tests does it quietly pass?
options: Reflexive (everyone groups with self), symmetric (A with B means B with A), transitive (A-B and B-C force A-C) — an equivalence relation
Only symmetry matters
Just pairing
Any grouping works
discovery.answer: Reflexive (everyone groups with self), symmetric (A with B means B with A), transitive (A-B and B-C force A-C) — an equivalence relation
discovery.hook: One counterexample kills a property — 'most pairs work' isn't a proof; but proving one requires the universal 'for all a' argument, not spot-checks. And x ≤ y² fails symmetry because squaring isn't order-preserving — nonlinearity breaks what intuition assumed.

c12_math_ch01.mission: Test relations like a verifier: check reflexive, symmetric, transitive on a pair-set, catch the single counterexample that breaks transitivity, and write the 'for all' language boards demand.
c12_math_ch01.finale: You can now prove or disprove a relation's properties — one counterexample to kill, a universal argument to keep.
c12_math_ch01.subtitle: Birth-month grouping passes all three tests — that's equivalence
c12_math_ch01.intro: A fair grouping rule turns out to be a precise mathematical object — three properties decide everything.
c12_math_ch01.goal: Verify reflexive, symmetric and transitive properties — counterexamples to disprove, universal arguments to prove.

discovery.question: 'The angle whose tangent is 1/12' has infinitely many answers — yet the ramp engineer needs exactly one. How do we force uniqueness?
options: Restrict the domain — chop sine, cosine, tangent to intervals where they're one-to-one, so each ratio maps to a single principal-value angle
Round the answer — take whichever decimal fits the drawing
Convert to degrees — one fixed unit system removes the ambiguity
Take the smallest positive angle — the principal value is just convention
discovery.answer: Restrict the domain — chop sine, cosine, tangent to intervals where they're one-to-one, so each ratio maps to a single principal-value angle
discovery.hook: The inverse's domain is the original's range and vice versa — that's why sec⁻¹ refuses |x|<1: sec never lands there. And tan⁻¹(−√3) is −π/3, not 2π/3: the answer must live inside the branch, not just satisfy the equation.

c12_math_ch02.mission: Lock each inverse to its branch: state all six domain-range pairs, compute principal values by asking which in-branch angle fits, and explain why sine and cosine picked different windows.
c12_math_ch02.finale: You can now see inverse trig as engineered uniqueness — where the branch interval is the whole point.
c12_math_ch02.subtitle: Infinitely many angles — the branch picks one
c12_math_ch02.intro: Every trig ratio hides infinitely many angles; the principal branch is the rule that chooses exactly one.
c12_math_ch02.goal: Master principal value branches — why restriction creates inverses and where each function's answer must live.

discovery.question: 40 students × 5 subjects = 200 marks. A list is chaos; a grid is a matrix. What does the 'order' 40×5 actually decide?
options: Everything downstream — rows×columns fix which operations are even legal later; order is a matrix's operating licence
Just the size
Which number is first
Nothing important
discovery.answer: Everything downstream — rows×columns fix which operations are even legal later; order is a matrix's operating licence
discovery.hook: Types aren't exclusive — the 1×1 matrix is simultaneously row, column, square, diagonal, scalar and identity. And 'they look the same' isn't equality: same order PLUS every corresponding element equal — both conditions, stated.

c12_math_ch03.mission: Build matrices from formulas: compute a_ij = (i−2j)² cell by cell, classify P and Q through the diagonal→scalar→identity chain, and write matrix equality the way the marking scheme wants it.
c12_math_ch03.finale: You can now read a matrix's order as its licence — and classify types that happily overlap in one little grid.
c12_math_ch03.subtitle: The 1×1 matrix is every type at once
c12_math_ch03.intro: A grid of numbers becomes powerful the moment its rows and columns get rules.
c12_math_ch03.goal: Read matrix order, build matrices from element formulas, and classify the seven types precisely.

discovery.question: Two pens and five notebooks cost ₹110; three pens and two cost ₹70. Before solving for prices, one number already promises a unique answer exists. Which?
options: The determinant — |A| = ad−bc = −11 ≠ 0 certifies the system won't collapse into contradiction or infinity
The total ₹180
The coefficient 2
The larger price
discovery.answer: The determinant — |A| = ad−bc = −11 ≠ 0 certifies the system won't collapse into contradiction or infinity
discovery.hook: Only square matrices earn a determinant — a 2×3 grid can't be expanded because the recursion needs equal rows and columns. And |A| isn't modulus: it can be negative, and a non-zero value is the green light for unique solutions.

c12_math_ch04.mission: Compute the gateway number: evaluate 2×2 determinants by ad−bc with the sign order right, expand a 3×3 along any row, and explain why every expansion converges on the same value.
c12_math_ch04.finale: You can now read a determinant as a solvability certificate — the single number that decides whether the system has one answer or none.
c12_math_ch04.subtitle: One number decides if the prices even exist
c12_math_ch04.intro: Before you solve a system, one scalar quietly tells you whether a unique solution exists at all.
c12_math_ch04.goal: Compute determinants of order 1, 2 and 3 — and understand why squareness is the entry fee.

discovery.question: A metro card's balance drops smoothly — until one station's glitch deducts ₹50 extra. That jump in the graph is a failure of exactly which equality?
options: lim x→c f(x) = f(c) — the limit must exist AND equal the function's value; a jump means left and right never agreed
f(c) exists — a defined value at the point is what continuity means
The limit exists — two-sided agreement alone guarantees continuity
The slope stays finite — a sharp corner, not a jump, is what breaks it
discovery.answer: lim x→c f(x) = f(c) — the limit must exist AND equal the function's value; a jump means left and right never agreed
discovery.hook: A limit existing isn't enough — (x²−1)/(x−1) has limit 2 at x=1 but f(1) doesn't exist, so it's discontinuous there. Three conditions, all required: defined value, existing limit, and the two being equal.

c12_math_ch05.mission: Verify continuity like an auditor: run all three conditions on piecewise functions, classify each break as removable, jump or infinite, and find the parameter that stitches a seam shut.
c12_math_ch05.finale: You can now prove a function continuous — or name exactly which of the three conditions broke and how.
c12_math_ch05.subtitle: The graph jumped — one equality failed
c12_math_ch05.intro: A function is continuous where its limit and its value shake hands — three conditions make the handshake official.
c12_math_ch05.goal: Verify continuity at a point via the three conditions and classify discontinuities by their left-right behaviour.

discovery.question: A balloon fills at 900 cm³/s, yet its radius slows as it grows. How do you find how fast the radius rises at r = 15?
options: Differentiate the relation in time — dV/dt = 4πr²·dr/dt links the known rate to the unknown; the chain rule does the connecting
Divide dV/dt by r — the growth rate scales inversely with radius
The radius rises constantly — a steady inflow means a steady rise
Measure dr/dt directly — rates can only be observed, never derived
discovery.answer: Differentiate the relation in time — dV/dt = 4πr²·dr/dt links the known rate to the unknown; the chain rule does the connecting
discovery.hook: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) works only while dx/dt ≠ 0 — derivatives aren't fractions to cancel blindly. And in the marginal-cost answer, ₹30.015 is mathematically right but wrong on a bill: currency wants ₹30.02 — context is part of the computation.

c12_math_ch06.mission: Link two moving quantities: set up related rates for ripples, cubes and conical tanks, keep units honest, and interpret what the rate's sign is saying.
c12_math_ch06.finale: You can now turn 'how fast is it changing' into an equation — chain rule as the bridge between what you know and what you need.
c12_math_ch06.subtitle: The balloon fills steadily — the radius doesn't
c12_math_ch06.intro: When two quantities share a clock, their rates are chained — learn to pull one through the other.
c12_math_ch06.goal: Apply the chain rule to related rates — geometric, physical and economic.

discovery.question: Velocity is the derivative of position — so given v(t) = 3t² + 2, where's the position? Why is the answer never a single function?
options: Run the derivative backwards — t³ + 2t works, but so does +C of any value; the family differs by where you started
Integrate to one answer
It's impossible
Add zero only
discovery.answer: Run the derivative backwards — t³ + 2t works, but so does +C of any value; the family differs by where you started
discovery.hook: The power rule dies at n = −1 — division by zero is why ∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C stands apart. And ∫e^{2x}dx isn't e^{2x}: the chain rule's inner 2 must be compensated, so it's ½e^{2x} + C. Verify by differentiating back.

c12_math_ch07.mission: Read every derivative formula backwards: integrate polynomials, spot where the power rule fails, catch the chain-rule compensation, and always prove it by re-differentiating.
c12_math_ch07.finale: You can now integrate as reverse differentiation — with the +C honouring every starting point the derivative erased.
c12_math_ch07.subtitle: Differentiation forgets the constant — integration must guess
c12_math_ch07.intro: Every derivative formula is a treasure map read backwards — and the +C marks all the starting points it erased.
c12_math_ch07.goal: Master indefinite integration as inverse differentiation — standard forms, +C, and verification.

discovery.question: ∫₀^2π sin x dx = 0 — so the area under one full sine wave is zero? What did the computation actually measure?
options: Net signed area — the positive hump cancelled the negative; true geometric area needs absolute values over each interval: 2 + 2 = 4
Zero is correct — the integral really does measure geometric area
π — the two half-wave areas are π each and cancel out
2π — over a full period the integral should equal the interval length
discovery.answer: Net signed area — the positive hump cancelled the negative; true geometric area needs absolute values over each interval: 2 + 2 = 4
discovery.hook: The integral is a limit of thin strips — each f(xᵢ)·Δx is a rectangle's area, and shrinking width to zero turns approximation into exactness. And the strip's direction follows the function: x = g(y) wants horizontal strips, not a forced re-solve.

c12_math_ch08.mission: Set up the area integral correctly: choose vertical or horizontal strips to match the function, split at the axis where the sign flips, and turn the answer into square units with meaning.
c12_math_ch08.finale: You can now read a definite integral as accumulated area — and catch the cancellation that hides real geometry.
c12_math_ch08.subtitle: The integral said zero; the area said four
c12_math_ch08.intro: A curved garden bed needs soil — and the integral that measures it is just a limit of thin strips.
c12_math_ch08.goal: Set up area-under-curve integrals with the right strip direction and the right sign handling.

discovery.question: 'd²y/dx² cubed, plus (dy/dx) to the fourth' — a student calls this order 4 because of the exponent. What's the actual order?
options: 2 — order is the highest derivative present, not the power it's raised to; exponents belong to degree, a different question entirely
4 — the highest power anywhere in the equation sets its order
3 — order counts the number of derivative terms present
1 — only the first derivative determines a differential equation's order
discovery.answer: 2 — order is the highest derivative present, not the power it's raised to; exponents belong to degree, a different question entirely
discovery.hook: A differential equation needs a derivative to be one — 'x² − 5x + 6 = 0' is just algebra. Cooling chai wrote the first one you'll meet: dT/dt = −k(T − T_room), order 1, because the rate of cooling depends on the temperature itself.

c12_math_ch09.mission: Interrogate any equation: decide if it's a differential equation, name the highest derivative for the order, and keep order versus degree separate in your head.
c12_math_ch09.finale: You can now read a differential equation's skeleton — derivative present, order named, ordinary versus partial sorted.
c12_math_ch09.subtitle: The exponent said 4 — the highest derivative said 2
c12_math_ch09.intro: Any law that says 'rate depends on the quantity' becomes a differential equation — first learn to read its skeleton.
c12_math_ch09.goal: Identify differential equations and their order — highest derivative rules, exponents don't.

discovery.question: A drone hovering still for five minutes has a displacement vector too — of length zero and no direction. Is it still a vector?
options: Yes — the zero vector: magnitude 0, direction undefined, and by convention collinear with everything
No — no direction
Only while hovering
It's a scalar
discovery.answer: Yes — the zero vector: magnitude 0, direction undefined, and by convention collinear with everything
discovery.hook: Same magnitude isn't equal vectors — 5 N east and 5 N north differ; equality needs direction too. And collinear doesn't mean same direction: parallel either way counts. Position doesn't matter — vectors are free to slide, defined by magnitude and direction alone.

c12_math_ch10.mission: Sort scalar from vector in the real world: classify speed versus velocity, draw a vector's negative and its unit, and prove two differently-placed arrows can be the same vector.
c12_math_ch10.finale: You can now speak vector precisely — magnitude AND direction, with the starting point deliberately irrelevant.
c12_math_ch10.subtitle: 5 N east ≠ 5 N north — direction is half the vector
c12_math_ch10.intro: Speed is a number; a delivery needs a direction. The difference is the entire subject of vectors.
c12_math_ch10.goal: Define vectors by magnitude and direction — and classify zero, unit, collinear, equal and negative correctly.

discovery.question: A line's direction ratios are 2, −3, 6 — so its direction cosines are... 2, −3, 6? What's missing?
options: Normalisation — divide by √(4+9+36)=7 to get 2/7, −3/7, 6/7; cosines are a unit vector's components and must satisfy l²+m²+n²=1
Nothing — direction ratios and direction cosines are the same triple
Absolute values — cosines are always positive lengths, never signed
The angles — cosines must be measured from inclinations, not computed
discovery.answer: Normalisation — divide by √(4+9+36)=7 to get 2/7, −3/7, 6/7; cosines are a unit vector's components and must satisfy l²+m²+n²=1
discovery.hook: Ratios are any proportional triple; cosines are the unique normalised version. And l is cos α, not α — (2/7, 3/7, 6/7) are cosines; the angles are cos⁻¹ of each. Proportional ratios mean parallel lines; the dot product's zero means perpendicular.

c12_math_ch11.mission: Program a drone's path in 3D: turn two points into direction ratios, normalise to cosines, verify the unit-square identity, and read parallel versus perpendicular off the numbers.
c12_math_ch11.finale: You can now steer a line in space with three numbers — and tell the cosine from the angle it encodes.
c12_math_ch11.subtitle: Ratios describe direction; cosines normalise it
c12_math_ch11.intro: A drone needs its heading as cosines against three axes — one identity keeps the math honest.
c12_math_ch11.goal: Compute direction cosines and ratios — and read parallel/perpendicular lines from them.

discovery.question: A baker could use all 20 kg of flour — but the constraint says 'at most.' Why does an LPP write ≤ instead of =?
options: Constraints are ceilings, not quotas — she may spend or store less; '=' would forbid every option that doesn't exhaust the resource
Equations are simpler
She must use all
≤ is a typo convention
discovery.answer: Constraints are ceilings, not quotas — she may spend or store less; '=' would forbid every option that doesn't exhaust the resource
discovery.hook: Forget x, y ≥ 0 and the feasible region leaks into negative production — non-negativity is a mandatory component, not a courtesy. And adding a constraint can only shrink the region: the optimum can stay or worsen, never improve.

c12_math_ch12.mission: Translate a business into math: name decision variables, write the linear objective, turn every resource limit into an inequality, and finish with the non-negativity that boards penalise for missing.
c12_math_ch12.finale: You can now formulate an LPP — and see each constraint as a wall of the region where the answer must live.
c12_math_ch12.subtitle: At most 20 kg — the inequality is the realism
c12_math_ch12.intro: Profit, flour, sugar and space — a bakery's daily puzzle becomes three inequalities and one line to maximise.
c12_math_ch12.goal: Formulate linear programming problems — variables, objective, constraints and the non-negativity floor.

discovery.question: Of 500 students, 200 study Physics and 100 study both. Told a student takes Physics, the chance they also take Math isn't 100/500 — why not?
options: The condition shrank the sample space — only the 200 Physics students count now, so it's 100/200; P(E|F) divides by P(F), renormalising to a world where F already happened
Because half took both
Math is harder
Random rounding
discovery.answer: The condition shrank the sample space — only the 200 Physics students count now, so it's 100/200; P(E|F) divides by P(F), renormalising to a world where F already happened
discovery.hook: P(A|B) and P(B|A) aren't twins — same numerator, different denominators. And 'P(E|F) = P(E)·P(F)' is an independence formula smuggled into a conditional problem; the right answer can be numerically lucky while the reasoning is wrong.

c12_math_ch13.mission: Condition a probability correctly: redraw the sample space after the given event, compute the renormalised ratio, and keep the direction of conditioning straight.
c12_math_ch13.finale: You can now update probability on new information — and see why the denominator, not the question, is what changed.
c12_math_ch13.subtitle: The denominator shrank — that's the whole trick
c12_math_ch13.intro: 'Given that...' is the most powerful two words in probability — it redraws the entire sample space.
c12_math_ch13.goal: Compute conditional probability by renormalising to the condition — and keep P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A) straight.

discovery.question: A neutron decays into a proton (+e) and an electron (−e) — two charged particles from a neutral one. Has charge conservation just been violated?
options: No — net charge is what conservation counts: 0 before, +e plus −e = 0 after; making charged particles isn't making charge
Yes — two charges appeared
Only protons count
Decay is exempt
discovery.answer: No — net charge is what conservation counts: 0 before, +e plus −e = 0 after; making charged particles isn't making charge
discovery.hook: Charge isn't continuous — q = ne means 1.5e can't exist on a body. And rubbing doesn't create charge; it moves electrons (which even carry a calculable, tiny mass) from wool to polythene — one body's deficit is the other's excess.

c12_phy_ch01.mission: Account for charge like a ledger: count electrons behind a rubbed rod's charge, split the total when identical spheres touch, and test '2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C' against quantization.
c12_phy_ch01.finale: You can now run charge as three laws — additive, conserved, quantized — and catch the conservation argument that confuses particles with net charge.
c12_phy_ch01.subtitle: Two charges were born — and zero charge was created
c12_phy_ch01.intro: Sparks from a winter sweater are a trillion-electron migration — and the ledger still balances to the last e.
c12_phy_ch01.goal: Apply additivity, conservation and quantization of charge to real transfers and decays.

discovery.question: Why must the test charge measuring potential be 'infinitesimal' and move 'without acceleration'? What breaks if it isn't?
options: A finite charge disturbs the source field being measured, and accelerating it sends work into kinetic energy instead of potential — the definition is an operational contract
Nothing breaks
It saves time
Bigger is better
discovery.answer: A finite charge disturbs the source field being measured, and accelerating it sends work into kinetic energy instead of potential — the definition is an operational contract
discovery.hook: Potential is a scalar even though the field is a vector — work is path-independent, so V can't carry direction. And V > 0 doesn't mean U > 0: a negative test charge in a positive potential has negative potential energy. Field and energy belong to different owners.

c12_phy_ch02.mission: Define potential the operational way: work per unit charge from infinity, no acceleration allowed; then read field direction as the direction potential falls, not 'flows.'
c12_phy_ch02.finale: You can now separate potential, potential difference and potential energy — three quantities students blur into one.
c12_phy_ch02.subtitle: Move it slowly or the number isn't potential
c12_phy_ch02.intro: Like a porter lifting a suitcase onto a shelf — the work per kilogram is gravitational potential; per coulomb, it's volts.
c12_phy_ch02.goal: Define electrostatic potential operationally — V = W/q, scalar, measured against infinity.

discovery.question: Electrons in your wire drift at millimetres per second — yet the bulb lights the instant you flip the switch. What's actually travelling fast?
options: The field — the electric field propagates near light-speed, nudging every electron into drift at once; the carriers crawl, the signal doesn't
Electrons sprint
Light fills the wire
Instant always
discovery.answer: The field — the electric field propagates near light-speed, nudging every electron into drift at once; the carriers crawl, the signal doesn't
discovery.hook: 'I = 5 C' is a category error — current is a rate, charge is an amount. And the arrow on the wire isn't a vector: currents add algebraically, not tip-to-tail. Conventional current runs opposite the electrons because it was named before anyone knew electrons existed.

c12_phy_ch03.mission: Correct the current confusions: compute charge from amps and seconds, weigh drift speed against carrier density in I = nAv_d, and explain why the scalar still gets an arrow.
c12_phy_ch03.finale: You can now read current as a rate with a historical arrow — and separate the crawling electrons from the racing field.
c12_phy_ch03.subtitle: The electrons crawl — the field sprints
c12_phy_ch03.intro: Your phone charger moves electrons at a crawl, yet responds instantly. The answer is what actually travels.
c12_phy_ch03.goal: Define current as dQ/dt — and untangle conventional direction, electron drift and the scalar arrow.

discovery.question: A magnet bends the electron beam in an old TV tube — yet the electrons never speed up or slow down. How can a force leave speed untouched?
options: It's perpendicular to velocity — F = qv×B steers without pushing; zero work, direction changed, kinetic energy conserved
It cancels gravity
Electrons resist
The field is weak
discovery.answer: It's perpendicular to velocity — F = qv×B steers without pushing; zero work, direction changed, kinetic energy conserved
discovery.hook: Same field, same speed: proton and electron feel equal force in opposite directions — but the electron accelerates ~1836 times harder because F = ma divides by mass. And the right-hand rule belongs to positive charge; flip it for electrons.

c12_phy_ch04.mission: Cross the vectors yourself: compute F = qvB sin θ for a proton at 30°, run the right-hand rule for both charge signs, and explain to a sceptic why magnetic force can never do work.
c12_phy_ch04.finale: You can now predict a charge's deflection — and defend the strange truth that a real force can do zero work.
c12_phy_ch04.subtitle: The force is real — the work is zero
c12_phy_ch04.intro: A bar magnet bends a beam of electrons — the first sign that magnetism only steers, never pushes.
c12_phy_ch04.goal: Apply the magnetic Lorentz force — magnitude, right-hand direction, and the zero-work consequence.

discovery.question: Cut a bar magnet in half to isolate its north pole — and you get two complete dipoles instead. What does that refusal tell you?
options: Magnetic field lines are closed loops — they continue S→N inside the magnet, so no isolated pole can ever exist
The cut was uneven
Poles hide inside
Iron is stubborn
discovery.answer: Magnetic field lines are closed loops — they continue S→N inside the magnet, so no isolated pole can ever exist
discovery.hook: Field lines aren't lines of force — the magnetic force is qv×B, perpendicular to the line. And two lines crossing would mean B has two directions at one point: impossible. Crowding shows strength; tangents show direction.

c12_phy_ch05.mission: Map a magnet honestly: sketch the closed loops inside and out, place a dipole in a field and compute both torque (mB sinθ) and energy (−mB cosθ) without swapping them.
c12_phy_ch05.finale: You can now read field lines as a vector field's portrait — loops that never end, density that means strength.
c12_phy_ch05.subtitle: You can't cut a magnet down to one pole
c12_phy_ch05.intro: Iron filings draw the pattern; the physics says the lines never start or stop — they loop through the magnet itself.
c12_phy_ch05.goal: Read bar-magnet field lines and dipole behaviour — closed loops, torque and potential energy.

discovery.question: Press the key and the galvanometer kicks; hold it pressed and the needle goes dead — same current flowing the whole time. What actually induces emf?
options: Change — a steady current gives steady flux and dΦ/dt = 0; only the rising or falling flux at press and release pushes emf
The current itself
The coil's heat
Contact sparks
discovery.answer: Change — a steady current gives steady flux and dΦ/dt = 0; only the rising or falling flux at press and release pushes emf
discovery.hook: Emf depends on the rate of change, not the amount — a bigger flux held constant induces nothing, a small flux flipped fast induces plenty. And flux is B·A cosθ: a 45° tilt quietly cuts your answer by √2.

c12_phy_ch06.mission: Induce an emf on purpose: compute flux with the cosθ intact, differentiate it against time for a decaying field, and predict the galvanometer's kick on press versus hold versus release.
c12_phy_ch06.finale: You can now read Faraday's law as a rate equation — where only changing flux makes electricity.
c12_phy_ch06.subtitle: Hold the key — and the emf vanishes
c12_phy_ch06.intro: A magnet at rest inside a coil does nothing; move it and the galvanometer jumps. Change is the ingredient.
c12_phy_ch06.goal: Apply Faraday's law — flux through a coil and emf from its rate of change.

discovery.question: Your wall socket is labelled 220 V AC — but the sine wave actually swings to +311 V. Which number is 'the voltage,' and why?
options: 220 V is the RMS — the DC-equivalent heating value; the real peak is 311 V, and every appliance rating silently speaks RMS
311 V is the rating
Average is zero
Both are equal
discovery.answer: 220 V is the RMS — the DC-equivalent heating value; the real peak is 311 V, and every appliance rating silently speaks RMS
discovery.hook: Average AC over a cycle is zero — but i²R is never negative, which is why heating still happens and why RMS exists. And mixing peak with RMS is the classic trap: a '200 V peak' source loses to a '150 V RMS' source on real power.

c12_phy_ch07.mission: Translate AC numbers honestly: convert peak and RMS both ways, compute a bulb's resistance and current on 220 V, and decide which mismatched source delivers more power.
c12_phy_ch07.finale: You can now read any AC rating — knowing it's the heating-equivalent, not the peak, the nameplate promises.
c12_phy_ch07.subtitle: 220 on the label, 311 at the peak
c12_phy_ch07.intro: The mains voltage is a wave swinging ±311 V — the number on the socket is its DC-equivalent for heating.
c12_phy_ch07.goal: Use RMS values — peak/√2 — and why power calculations live on RMS, not peak.

discovery.question: Inside a charging capacitor, no charge crosses the gap — yet a compass needle between the plates still deflects. Where is the 'current'?
options: In the changing field — a time-varying electric flux acts exactly like a current, i_d = ε₀ dΦE/dt, and produces real magnetism
Charges tunnel across
The compass is wrong
Stray wire field
discovery.answer: In the changing field — a time-varying electric flux acts exactly like a current, i_d = ε₀ dΦE/dt, and produces real magnetism
discovery.hook: Ampere's law gave two answers for one point until Maxwell fixed it — a loop through the wire saw current, a loop through the gap saw none, yet B must be unique. Displacement current isn't a trick; the field it makes deflects needles identically.

c12_phy_ch08.mission: Repair Ampere's law yourself: find the contradiction between two surfaces on one loop, compute a displacement current from a sinusoidal field, and defend why i_d is as real as conduction current.
c12_phy_ch08.finale: You can now see Maxwell's fix — the symmetry that says changing E makes B, and the gap conducts 'current' without a single charge crossing.
c12_phy_ch08.subtitle: No charges crossed — the needle still moved
c12_phy_ch08.intro: Current flows to the capacitor plates and stops — but the magnetic field doesn't notice the gap.
c12_phy_ch08.goal: Understand displacement current — the missing term that made Ampere's law consistent.

discovery.question: A concave mirror's focal length is written +15 cm — and the mirror equation now predicts a virtual image where a real one should be. What went wrong?
options: The sign convention — f and R are negative for concave because focus and centre sit against the incident light; one flipped sign flips the image's nature
Rounding error
Mirror is convex
Focus is behind
discovery.answer: The sign convention — f and R are negative for concave because focus and centre sit against the incident light; one flipped sign flips the image's nature
discovery.hook: The mirror's normal isn't drawn at random — it always runs through the centre of curvature, which is why a parallel ray bounces through focus and why f = R/2 exists at all. And the sign convention isn't bookkeeping: it encodes whether the focus is real or virtual.

c12_phy_ch09.mission: Apply the Cartesian rules without mercy: assign signs to u, v, f, R for both mirror types, verify f = R/2 with a sun-and-screen measurement, and trace how one wrong sign corrupts the whole equation.
c12_phy_ch09.finale: You can now run mirror math on convention, not memory — where every sign is a statement about real versus virtual.
c12_phy_ch09.subtitle: One flipped sign flipped the image's nature
c12_phy_ch09.intro: The car's side mirror shrinks the world for a reason — and the sign convention is the language that says it.
c12_phy_ch09.goal: Master the laws of reflection and Cartesian sign convention — including why f = R/2 carries a sign.

discovery.question: Light enters glass and bends toward the normal — Newton's particles predicted the opposite, yet Huygens' wavelets got it right in 1678. What does the geometry force?
options: Slower wavelets tilt the front — with v₂ < v₁ the inner wavelet is smaller, so the envelope must swing toward the normal: sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂
Light gets heavier
Glass pulls rays
Density absorbs speed
discovery.answer: Slower wavelets tilt the front — with v₂ < v₁ the inner wavelet is smaller, so the envelope must swing toward the normal: sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂
discovery.hook: Every point on a wavefront is a new source — and the next wavefront is the forward envelope of all their ripples. The backward wave was Huygens' awkward patch: he declared its amplitude zero by hand, and modern theory only later showed it cancels by phase.

c12_phy_ch10.mission: Construct propagation by hand: place secondary sources on a wavefront, draw wavelets of radius vΔt, and tangent-envelope your way to the new front — spherical and plane.
c12_phy_ch10.finale: You can now build wave propagation geometrically — and watch refraction emerge as a speed difference, not a rule.
c12_phy_ch10.subtitle: Each point ripples — the envelope is the future
c12_phy_ch10.intro: A pebble's rings on a pond are wavefronts; Huygens said every point on each ring starts the next one.
c12_phy_ch10.goal: Apply Huygens' principle — secondary wavelets, forward envelopes, and refraction from speed contrast.

discovery.question: Blast zinc with a blinding white torch — nothing. Shine a feeble UV lamp — electrons pour out instantly. What is light actually delivering?
options: Frequency — each photon carries hν; below threshold no intensity helps because energy arrives in packets, not a continuous wash
More light overall
Heat buildup
UV is stronger
discovery.answer: Frequency — each photon carries hν; below threshold no intensity helps because energy arrives in packets, not a continuous wash
discovery.hook: Brighter light means more electrons, not faster ones — doubling intensity doubles saturation current but leaves stopping potential untouched. K_max answers to frequency alone: that's the result wave theory can never explain, and the graph where the curves split.

c12_phy_ch11.mission: Run the photoelectric experiment mentally: predict how photocurrent shifts with intensity versus frequency, hold stopping potential against brighter light, and spot the 'yellow beats green' report that can't be true.
c12_phy_ch11.finale: You can now read the photoelectric evidence — and see exactly where the wave picture broke and the photon was forced on physics.
c12_phy_ch11.subtitle: Brighter didn't help — bluer did
c12_phy_ch11.intro: A solar calculator and a dusk-sensing streetlight run on the same shock: light ejects electrons by frequency, not brightness.
c12_phy_ch11.goal: Interpret photoelectric experiments — threshold frequency, stopping potential, and intensity's real role.

discovery.question: A cannonball fired at tissue paper bounced straight back — that's how Rutherford described 1-in-8000 alphas reversing off gold foil. What did the rebound prove?
options: Almost all the mass and all the positive charge sit in a nucleus ~10⁻¹⁵ m wide — the atom is mostly empty space, so most alphas sail through
Gold is elastic
Alphas are light
Foil was defective
discovery.answer: Almost all the mass and all the positive charge sit in a nucleus ~10⁻¹⁵ m wide — the atom is mostly empty space, so most alphas sail through
discovery.hook: The scattering angle maps the aim: smaller impact parameter means closer approach and bigger deflection, and a head-on shot converts all kinetic energy to Coulomb potential — that's what measures nuclear size. And the foil had to be thin — 750 atomic layers — so single scattering, not statistical blur, told the truth.

c12_phy_ch12.mission: Recreate the discovery: link impact parameter to scattering angle, derive the distance of closest approach from energy conservation, and compute the nucleus's upper bound for 7.7 MeV alphas on gold.
c12_phy_ch12.finale: You can now read a scattering pattern as a map of the atom — mostly void, one dense kernel, one formula to size it.
c12_phy_ch12.subtitle: The tissue paper shot back a cannonball
c12_phy_ch12.intro: Most alphas passed through gold like it was empty — because it is. The few that bounced back found the nucleus.
c12_phy_ch12.goal: Interpret Rutherford scattering — impact parameter, closest approach and the nuclear model.

discovery.question: No chlorine atom weighs 35.46 u — yet the periodic table insists it does. Where does that number live?
options: In the average — it's the weighted mean of chlorine's isotopes (³⁵Cl at ~75%, ³⁷Cl at ~25%), a property of the sample, not any single atom
In every atom
Half a neutron
Rounding error
discovery.answer: In the average — it's the weighted mean of chlorine's isotopes (³⁵Cl at ~75%, ³⁷Cl at ~25%), a property of the sample, not any single atom
discovery.hook: Mass number and atomic mass are different objects — A is the integer count of nucleons in one nucleus; atomic mass is the averaged decimal of all isotopes. And the triple classification is strict: same Z isotopes, same A isobars, same N isotones.

c12_phy_ch13.mission: Read a nuclide symbol like a licence plate: extract Z, A and N, classify pairs as isotopes/isobars/isotones, and compute the mass defect hiding inside ⁵⁶Fe.
c12_phy_ch13.finale: You can now decode any nuclide — and keep the integer count of one nucleus separate from the decimal average of a sample.
c12_phy_ch13.subtitle: No chlorine atom is 35.46 — the average is
c12_phy_ch13.intro: The periodic table's decimal is a statistical ghost — no atom carries it, yet it describes them all.
c12_phy_ch13.goal: Decode nuclide notation — Z, A, N — and separate mass number from atomic mass, isotopes from isobars from isotones.

discovery.question: At absolute zero a silicon chip is a perfect insulator — yet at room temperature it powers your phone. What changed without adding a single atom?
options: Heat — kT ≈ 25 meV nudges electrons across the ~1 eV gap, creating mobile electrons AND holes; cold silicon simply has no carriers to move
Voltage appears
Atoms rearrange
Impurities grow
discovery.answer: Heat — kT ≈ 25 meV nudges electrons across the ~1 eV gap, creating mobile electrons AND holes; cold silicon simply has no carriers to move
discovery.hook: One part per million of arsenic floods silicon with electrons — and the mass-action law n_e·n_h = n_i² quietly strangles the holes to compensate. The gap size sorts the world: zero is a metal, ~1 eV a semiconductor, above ~3 eV an insulator — same atoms, different bands.

c12_phy_ch14.mission: Classify a solid by its band gap: sketch the three band diagrams, explain why diamond's structure hides an insulator, and compute majority/minority carriers in doped silicon.
c12_phy_ch14.finale: You can now read a solid's conductivity from its band diagram — and see doping as a tilted balance the mass-action law enforces.
c12_phy_ch14.subtitle: Cold silicon insulates; warm silicon computes
c12_phy_ch14.intro: Copper, plastic, silicon — same kind of stuff, wildly different behaviour. The difference is an energy gap.
c12_phy_ch14.goal: Read energy bands — valence, conduction, gap — and how doping rewrites carrier counts.

discovery.question: Rohan is loud and funny with friends, quiet and respectful at the school assembly. Did his personality change — or did something else move?
options: The situation — situationism says context can override traits; the aggressive go submissive before a boss, the talkative go quiet in assembly
His traits reset — personality permanently shifts with each audience
He is performing — the quiet assembly version is deliberate masking
Two personalities — one for peers and one for authority figures
discovery.answer: The situation — situationism says context can override traits; the aggressive go submissive before a boss, the talkative go quiet in assembly
discovery.hook: Nature versus nurture isn't a contest — heredity sets a reaction range, environment picks where inside it you land. Modern psychology is interactionist: the honest answer to 'trait or situation?' is both, dynamically.

c12_psy_ch01.mission: Analyse why classmates differ: run the trait-versus-situation debate on real behaviour, place heredity and environment in the same frame, and resist the urge to crown either one.
c12_psy_ch01.finale: You can now read individual differences as an interaction — traits meeting situations, nature setting the range nurture navigates.
c12_psy_ch01.subtitle: Same Rohan, different room — trait or situation?
c12_psy_ch01.intro: Why does one friend race through the test while another barely finishes? The answer is older than the classroom.
c12_psy_ch01.goal: Explain individual differences through the trait-situation debate and nature-nurture interaction.

discovery.question: 'I am honest, a Hindu, a classical dancer, a daughter.' A student files 'honest' under social identity and 'Hindu' under personal. What's backwards?
options: The criterion — personal identity is what individuates you (honest, dancer); social identity is group membership (Hindu, daughter). They swapped them
Both are social
Hindu is personal
Dancer is social
discovery.answer: The criterion — personal identity is what individuates you (honest, dancer); social identity is group membership (Hindu, daughter). They swapped them
discovery.hook: The self is both the writer and the written — 'I am studying' is subject; 'I am a student who procrastinates' is object. And the Indian self-boundary shifts: it expands to include family at a festival, contracts to career in an interview — context moves the border, not the self.

c12_psy_ch02.mission: Map a self-description: split personal from social identity, catch subject and object working in one sentence, and weigh how fixed versus shifting boundaries turn family-over-career into guilt in one culture and fulfilment in another.
c12_psy_ch02.finale: You can now dissect 'who am I' into its parts — and see the boundary around 'I' as something culture taught you to draw.
c12_psy_ch02.subtitle: The self that writes and the self that's written
c12_psy_ch02.intro: You wrote 'describe yourself in 50 words' — and smuggled in two kinds of identity and a dual role for the self.
c12_psy_ch02.goal: Distinguish personal from social identity — and the self as subject and object across cultures.

discovery.question: Same board-exam date sheet: Priya's stomach knots in dread, Arjun opens a planner. If the event is identical, where does the stress actually live?
options: In the transaction — stress is the appraisal of demand against coping resources, not the event itself; same stressor, different strain
In the date sheet
In personalities only
In preparation
discovery.answer: In the transaction — stress is the appraisal of demand against coping resources, not the event itself; same stressor, different strain
discovery.hook: 'Eliminate distress, keep only eustress' fails twice — stress isn't binary, and too little arousal leaves you listless; a threat and a challenge can be the same event appraised differently. And the stressor ending doesn't end the strain — appraisal and arousal stay linked.

c12_psy_ch03.mission: Trace one stressful event through the model: name stressor and strain, separate primary from secondary appraisal, and argue why 'it's all in your personality' or 'all in the event' both miss the transaction.
c12_psy_ch03.finale: You can now locate stress where it actually lives — in the appraisal loop between a demand and your sense of coping.
c12_psy_ch03.subtitle: Same exam date — one dreads it, one plans for it
c12_psy_ch03.intro: Two students, one date sheet, two opposite reactions — stress lives in the appraisal, not the event.
c12_psy_ch03.goal: Define stress transactionally — stressor, appraisal, strain — and split eustress from distress.

discovery.question: A traffic policeman waves his arms wildly at an intersection; a pedestrian does the same on a quiet sidewalk. Same motion — why is only one maybe abnormal?
options: Context — deviance is judged against the role and the norm; the policeman's waving is prescribed by his job, the pedestrian's violates the unstated rule of calm public movement
The uniform exempts him — officials cannot be deviant while on duty
Both are abnormal — wild arm-waving is deviant wherever it occurs
Neither is abnormal — free movement covers both actions equally
discovery.answer: Context — deviance is judged against the role and the norm; the policeman's waving is prescribed by his job, the pedestrian's violates the unstated rule of calm public movement
discovery.hook: The Four Ds aren't a checklist demanding all four — deviance, distress and dysfunction together usually suffice without danger. And 'weird = abnormal' fails: a ritual or a job can license behaviour that looks deviant but functions perfectly — the maladaptive lens asks whether it blocks a life.

c12_psy_ch04.mission: Judge a case like a clinician: run Meena's school-silence through each D, weigh deviance against maladaptiveness, and catch where context turns 'strange' into 'sanctioned.'
c12_psy_ch04.finale: You can now define abnormality as a cluster judged by culture and function — not by how unusual it looks.
c12_psy_ch04.subtitle: Same arm-waving — one is a job, one is a symptom
c12_psy_ch04.intro: Two students before exams — one studies hard, one can't open a book. The line between them has four letters.
c12_psy_ch04.goal: Apply the Four Ds and the social-norms versus maladaptive lenses to judge abnormal behaviour.

discovery.question: 'I understand exactly — I failed my boards too.' A therapist says this with warmth, and it's still the wrong response. What's missing?
options: Empathy — feeling like the client, not for them; sharing your own story is sympathy, which pulls the focus off the client's experience
Nothing — warmth plus shared experience is textbook empathy
More concrete advice — the client needs solutions, not stories
A diagnosis first — feelings cannot be addressed before labels
discovery.answer: Empathy — feeling like the client, not for them; sharing your own story is sympathy, which pulls the focus off the client's experience
discovery.hook: Therapy isn't 'paid friendship' — the frame does the healing: a contract with goals, a limited duration, confidentiality with teeth, and regard that doesn't depend on the client pleasing you. 'Any caring teacher with a book' misses that training under supervision is a requirement, not a bonus.

c12_psy_ch05.mission: Build the therapeutic alliance from a first session: map '12 weekly sessions' and 'confidential unless harm' onto their components, and separate empathy from the sympathy that sounds identical.
c12_psy_ch05.finale: You can now see the therapeutic relationship as engineered — boundaries, contract and empathy doing the work friendship can't.
c12_psy_ch05.subtitle: It sounded like empathy — it was sympathy
c12_psy_ch05.intro: A friend says 'don't worry.' A therapist asks you to notice the catastrophic thought. The frame is the difference.
c12_psy_ch05.goal: Define psychotherapy's structure — goals, characteristics, and the alliance's contract, duration and empathy.

discovery.question: Riya knows exercise is essential and feels great doing it — yet never exercises. Does she have a positive attitude toward it?
options: Yes — attitude is a latent A-B-C system; her behavioural component is weak but cognition and affect are strong, so the attitude exists, just misaligned
No — no action
Only halfway
It's a belief
discovery.answer: Yes — attitude is a latent A-B-C system; her behavioural component is weak but cognition and affect are strong, so the attitude exists, just misaligned
discovery.hook: Knowing isn't an attitude — 'I know junk food is unhealthy' is only the cognitive third. And a lecture on benefits rarely builds durable attitudes; an experience that engages feeling and doing builds consonance across all three components.

c12_psy_ch06.mission: Dissect attitudes into A-B-C: find the weak component in a real scenario, separate belief from value from attitude, and choose the strategy that builds a lasting one.
c12_psy_ch06.finale: You can now read an attitude as three forces — and diagnose which one is dragging when belief and action diverge.
c12_psy_ch06.subtitle: She believes it, feels it — and still doesn't do it
c12_psy_ch06.intro: Think, feel, do — an attitude is all three at once, and they're rarely in perfect agreement.
c12_psy_ch06.goal: Apply the A-B-C model of attitudes — and why components can disagree without the attitude vanishing.

discovery.question: Thousands scream for the same band at a concert — and if your neighbour leaves, nothing changes for you. Why isn't that a group?
options: No interdependence or roles — a crowd shares a moment, not a fate; a group needs mutual dependence, roles, norms and a felt 'we'
Too many people
They came alone
Noise isn't shared
discovery.answer: No interdependence or roles — a crowd shares a moment, not a fate; a group needs mutual dependence, roles, norms and a felt 'we'
discovery.hook: 'All teams are groups, but not all groups are teams' — a family is a group without complementary skills or mutual accountability; a project where the leader does everything is a group failing to be a team. Structure and interdependence, not proximity, make the group.

c12_psy_ch07.mission: Sort real collections by the five criteria: label a metro queue, a student council, spectators and a cricket XI — then design the minimal-group experiment that creates bias from nothing.
c12_psy_ch07.finale: You can now tell a gathering from a group — and see that 'we' is built from interdependence, not headcount.
c12_psy_ch07.subtitle: Same stadium, same scream — still not a group
c12_psy_ch07.intro: A project team where one member's silence stalls everyone is a group; a concert audience isn't. The difference is structure.
c12_psy_ch07.goal: Apply the five criteria of a group — and distinguish it from crowd, team and audience.

discovery.question: In 1948 the USSR sealed every road into West Berlin — and the Allies flew in food for a year instead of fighting. Why didn't blockade become war?
options: Brinkmanship — shooting down supply planes risked nuclear WWIII, so both sides calibrated conflict short of direct battle; that restraint IS the Cold War
Airlift was faster
Berlin didn't matter
UN banned it
discovery.answer: Brinkmanship — shooting down supply planes risked nuclear WWIII, so both sides calibrated conflict short of direct battle; that restraint IS the Cold War
discovery.hook: 'Natural enemies' is too easy — they were wartime allies; the Cold War was made by post-war choices: imposed regimes in Poland, the atomic monopoly, mutual misread intentions. And the Iron Curtain was a metaphor for six years before it became a wall in 1961.

c12_ps_ch01.mission: Trace the alliance's collapse: weigh two post-war visions of Europe, decode the Berlin airlift as calibrated confrontation, and test 'inevitable rivalry' against the 1945–47 record.
c12_ps_ch01.finale: You can now read the Cold War's origin as choices, not fate — a war fought everywhere except between the two capitals.
c12_ps_ch01.subtitle: They blockaded a city — and chose airlift over war
c12_ps_ch01.intro: Two allies beat Hitler together, then spent 44 years pointing missiles at each other. The wall didn't start as one.
c12_ps_ch01.goal: Explain the Cold War's origins — ideological blocs, the Iron Curtain, and conflict kept just short of war.

discovery.question: The Soviet constitution guaranteed universal suffrage and civil liberties — and the country ran as a one-party state anyway. How did both hold at once?
options: Article 6 made the CPSU the constitutional 'leading force' — elections offered one candidate, real power ran through the party hierarchy, not the elected soviets
The constitution was ignored
People didn't vote
Rights came later
discovery.answer: Article 6 made the CPSU the constitutional 'leading force' — elections offered one candidate, real power ran through the party hierarchy, not the elected soviets
discovery.hook: India's Five-Year Plans weren't the Soviet model — Gosplan set binding targets for every enterprise and owned all industry; India's Planning Commission set indicative targets while markets and private ownership lived on. Inspiration isn't replication — and the Soviet system's early industrial miracle coexisted with the stagnation that later forced reform.

c12_ps_ch02.mission: Dissect a system that planned everything: separate comprehensive central planning from India's indicative version, compare the nomenklatura with the civil service, and weigh industrial triumph against consumer shortage.
c12_ps_ch02.finale: You can now read the Soviet system as two pillars — party monopoly and command economy — that mobilised fast and innovated poorly.
c12_ps_ch02.subtitle: The constitution promised rights — Article 6 promised the party
c12_ps_ch02.intro: One party, one plan, five-year targets for every factory — a system that built a superpower and then stalled.
c12_ps_ch02.goal: Explain the Soviet system — single-party rule plus central planning — and why it rose fast and stagnated.

discovery.question: In 1991 a hegemon had unmatched force — yet still queued at the UN for Resolution 678 before striking Iraq. Why bother?
options: Legitimacy multiplies power — UN cover built a 34-nation coalition including Arab states and showed hegemony as rule-shaping, not just force
The UN legally required it — force without a mandate is void
US forces were overstretched — allies supplied the missing troops
Coalitions are cheap — partners pay for the privilege of joining
discovery.answer: Legitimacy multiplies power — UN cover built a 34-nation coalition including Arab states and showed hegemony as rule-shaping, not just force
discovery.hook: Don't merge 1991 with 2003 — the first had a UN mandate and broad Arab participation; the second ran on a thin 'coalition of the willing' against allied protest. And it wasn't just oil: the US restored Kuwait's sovereignty and left — collective security, not seizure, was the public logic.

c12_ps_ch03.mission: Read the unipolar moment: connect precision weapons and live TV war to a revolution in military affairs, then weigh what UN authorization bought that unilateral force couldn't.
c12_ps_ch03.finale: You can now see 1991 as hegemony exercised through institutions — and the sharp contrast when that legitimacy was skipped in 2003.
c12_ps_ch03.subtitle: The superpower that asked permission first
c12_ps_ch03.intro: The first televised war showed missiles hitting targets live — and a hegemon that still wanted the UN's signature.
c12_ps_ch03.goal: Analyse the First Gulf War — UN legitimation, coalition-building and the display of unipolar military dominance.

discovery.question: In 1950, France offered to hand control of its coal and steel — the very materials armies run on — to a shared authority with Germany, its enemy of three wars. Why would a victor volunteer to disarm itself?
options: Pooling war-critical resources made war 'materially impossible' — neither side could re-arm secretly
France was too weak to refuse American pressure
It was purely a trade deal with no security motive
Germany demanded it as a condition of occupation ending
discovery.answer: Pooling war-critical resources made war 'materially impossible' — neither side could re-arm secretly
discovery.hook: Students assume the EU began with the Maastricht Treaty in 1992 — actually it was built stepwise from the 1951 coal-steel pool through the 1957 common market to a union that kept economics supranational but foreign policy intergovernmental.

c12_ps_ch04.mission: Trace each treaty from coal and steel to Maastricht, and decide at every step which slice of sovereignty states pooled — and why they refused to pool foreign policy the same way.
c12_ps_ch04.finale: You can now explain why Europe integrated economics by majority vote but kept war-and-peace decisions unanimous — and why that makes the EU a union of states, not a federal superstate.
c12_ps_ch04.subtitle: The trade deal designed to make war impossible
c12_ps_ch04.intro: Twenty-seven countries now make binding laws together — because in 1950 someone decided to make war materially impossible instead of just forbidden.
c12_ps_ch04.goal: Sequence the EU's treaty-by-treaty evolution and distinguish supranational community method from intergovernmental pillars.

discovery.question: The Indus Waters Treaty has survived three India-Pakistan wars, yet SAARC — created to cooperate on everything — can barely hold a summit. Why does the narrow deal outlast the grand one?
options: The water treaty decouples a survival resource from politics with binding technical rules and a neutral broker, while SAARC's consensus rule lets any bilateral feud veto everything
SAARC members simply lack political will
The water treaty works because India and Pakistan are friends on water
SAARC failed because South Asia shares nothing in common
discovery.answer: The water treaty decouples a survival resource from politics with binding technical rules and a neutral broker, while SAARC's consensus rule lets any bilateral feud veto everything
discovery.hook: Don't blame 'ancient religious hatreds' — South Asia's conflicts are post-Partition state-building failures: a hastily drawn border, majoritarian nation-building and a giant neighbour whose defensive moves read as threats to everyone smaller.

c12_ps_ch05.mission: Map South Asia's fault lines from Partition onward — Kashmir, water, nuclear rivalry — and test why cooperation keeps failing where the security dilemma runs deepest.
c12_ps_ch05.finale: You can now explain why shared rivers and shared history haven't produced a South Asian EU — and why institutional design, not goodwill, decides which deals survive.
c12_ps_ch05.subtitle: Eight neighbours, one Partition, and the deals that refuse to die
c12_ps_ch05.intro: A family that inherited one house and argues over every room boundary — that's South Asia after 1947.
c12_ps_ch05.goal: Explain how Partition structured South Asian conflict and why asymmetric distrust defeats regional cooperation.

discovery.question: The UN has no army, can't tax anyone, and runs on a budget a mid-sized government would call pocket change — so why do even superpowers keep funding it and showing up?
options: Standing rules, monitoring and permanent forums make cooperation cheaper and more predictable than renegotiating every crisis alone
Because the UN can legally compel any state to obey
Tradition — states attend out of habit, not interest
Small states fund it; big states merely tolerate it
discovery.answer: Standing rules, monitoring and permanent forums make cooperation cheaper and more predictable than renegotiating every crisis alone
discovery.hook: The UN is not a world government — it cannot draft soldiers, levy taxes or legislate, and its resolutions bind only because member states agreed to accept them. It's a cooperation machine built by sovereign states, not a sovereign over them.

c12_ps_ch06.mission: Diagnose the collective-action problems — free-riding, uncoordinated bans, unfunded public goods — that no state can fix alone, and match each to what an international organisation actually does.
c12_ps_ch06.finale: You can now explain why globalisation increases the need for international organisations instead of shrinking it — and why the Paris climate deal chose voluntary pledges over unenforceable targets.
c12_ps_ch06.subtitle: Why sovereign states build clubs they then complain about
c12_ps_ch06.intro: A virus ignores borders; a finance minister cannot. Something has to bridge that gap — and it isn't a world government.
c12_ps_ch06.goal: Explain why states create international organisations and how design choices solve collective-action problems without enforcement power.

discovery.question: A foreign intelligence agency crashes India's banking system with ransomware, and Maoist fighters hold 'liberated zones' in Chhattisgarh. Traditional security counts only one of these as its kind of threat — which, and why?
options: The Maoist insurgency — traditional security covers armed challenges to the state's monopoly on force, while cyberattacks fall outside its kinetic paradigm
The cyberattack — any foreign attack is an external threat
Both — anything dangerous is a traditional threat
Neither — traditional security only covers declared wars
discovery.answer: The Maoist insurgency — traditional security covers armed challenges to the state's monopoly on force, while cyberattacks fall outside its kinetic paradigm
discovery.hook: Students stretch 'internal threat' to mean any domestic problem — protests, corruption, communal riots. Traditional security counts only organised armed violence challenging the state's monopoly on force or its territory; farmer protests were dissent, not insurgency.

c12_ps_ch07.mission: Sort real crises — Kargil, Naxalism, Galwan, a bank hack — into external and internal traditional threats, and test where the military-first framework stops working.
c12_ps_ch07.finale: You can now define security the way a general does — state, sovereignty, armed force — and see exactly which 21st-century dangers slip through that frame.
c12_ps_ch07.subtitle: Tanks at the border, rebels in the forest — one old idea of 'threat'
c12_ps_ch07.intro: Kargil and Naxalism look nothing alike — yet one framework treats both as the same species of danger.
c12_ps_ch07.goal: Distinguish external from internal threats in the traditional, state-centric security framework and identify its limits.

discovery.question: On 15 August 1947, millions in Punjab and Bengal literally did not know which country they were waking up in. How did a border get drawn over 14 million people without them knowing?
options: A British lawyer who had never visited India drew district-level lines by religious majority in weeks, and the award was published after independence
The boundary followed ancient provincial borders everyone knew
