People chose their country by referendum district by district
The line was agreed by Congress and the League years earlier
discovery.answer: A British lawyer who had never visited India drew district-level lines by religious majority in weeks, and the award was published after independence
discovery.hook: Partition wasn't ancient hatred finally boiling over — decades of Hindu-Muslim cooperation preceded it. It was built in the 1940s: a failed federal compromise, a hasty British exit, and a mechanical map exercise that split villages and canal systems.

c12_ps_ch08.mission: Trace the chain from the 1940 Lahore Resolution through the collapsed Cabinet Mission Plan to the Radcliffe Line — and test whether Partition actually solved the communal problem it claimed to fix.
c12_ps_ch08.finale: You can now argue why Partition solved nothing it promised — it left more Muslims in India than in West Pakistan and created two minority problems — and why India answered it with a secular constitution.
c12_ps_ch08.subtitle: A line drawn in weeks, a wound measured in generations
c12_ps_ch08.intro: Freedom at midnight came with a footnote nobody read: the map arrived after the flags did.
c12_ps_ch08.goal: Analyse the political choices behind Partition, the Radcliffe Award's structural flaws, and the secular constitutional response.

discovery.question: In 1952, 53 parties and nearly 1,900 independents contested India's first election — yet one party took 74% of seats on just 45% of votes, then did it twice more. Rigged, or something stranger?
options: Democratic but lopsided: Congress's freedom-movement network and all-embracing coalition won pluralities seat after seat while a divided opposition split the rest under first-past-the-post
Rigged — opposition parties were effectively banned
Voters had no real choice on the ballot
Congress won because it controlled the Election Commission
discovery.answer: Democratic but lopsided: Congress's freedom-movement network and all-embracing coalition won pluralities seat after seat while a divided opposition split the rest under first-past-the-post
discovery.hook: One-party dominance is not a one-party system — China banned rivals; India didn't. Congress was so broad it housed left, right and centre in one tent, so its own factions did the job an opposition normally does.

c12_ps_ch09.mission: Dissect the 'Congress system': how a nationalist movement became a party that was simultaneously the government and its own opposition — and why rivals still couldn't break through.
c12_ps_ch09.finale: You can now explain dominance without dictatorship — and how first-past-the-post turns a 45% vote into a three-quarters majority.
c12_ps_ch09.subtitle: The party that contained its own opposition
c12_ps_ch09.intro: India's first elections had plenty of opposition parties — they just kept losing to an organisation built over sixty years of freedom struggle.
c12_ps_ch09.goal: Analyse how Congress's social and ideological coalition plus factionalism sustained democratic one-party dominance.

discovery.question: In 1944, eight of India's biggest industrialists signed a plan demanding the government run heavy industry — capitalists begging for state control. What were they thinking?
options: They lacked the capital and technology for heavy industry themselves, so they wanted the state to bear the risk — planning was a cross-ideological consensus, not a leftist imposition
The British forced them to endorse planning
They were secret socialists
It was a publicity stunt with no real intent
discovery.answer: They lacked the capital and technology for heavy industry themselves, so they wanted the state to bear the risk — planning was a cross-ideological consensus, not a leftist imposition
discovery.hook: The Planning Commission appears nowhere in the Constitution — it was created by an executive resolution and was only 'advisory', yet its control over plan funds made it arguably the most powerful extra-constitutional body in India for six decades.

c12_ps_ch10.mission: Reconstruct why a poor, newly free country chose five-year plans — and how a merely advisory body ended up steering where the money went.
c12_ps_ch10.finale: You can now explain the plan budget vs non-plan budget split, and why 'advisory' on paper meant decisive in practice.
c12_ps_ch10.subtitle: The powerful institution the Constitution never mentions
c12_ps_ch10.intro: Industrialists asking for a planned economy — in 1950s India, even capital agreed the market alone couldn't build a nation.
c12_ps_ch10.goal: Explain the Planning Commission's mandate, constitutional status and the Directive Principles logic behind India's planned development.

discovery.question: In 1956 India slammed Britain and France over Suez — then went quiet when Soviet tanks rolled into Hungary weeks later. If non-alignment meant neutrality, what explains that?
options: Non-alignment was never neutrality — it meant judging each issue independently rather than voting with a bloc, and India's choices reflected that
India was secretly pro-Soviet all along
Nehru simply didn't know about Hungary
India stayed neutral but the West complained louder
discovery.answer: Non-alignment was never neutrality — it meant judging each issue independently rather than voting with a bloc, and India's choices reflected that
discovery.hook: Students equate non-alignment with sitting out. Nehru's India took sides constantly — just never a bloc's side — and collected steel plants from the USSR and food aid from the US while refusing both alliances.

c12_ps_ch11.mission: Test non-alignment against its hardest cases — Bandung, Panchsheel, Suez, Hungary, and finally the 1962 war with the country India had just signed 'peaceful coexistence' with.
c12_ps_ch11.finale: You can now defend non-alignment as a strategy of independent judgment, not fence-sitting — and weigh honestly what it cost in 1962.
c12_ps_ch11.subtitle: Friendly to both camps, married to neither
c12_ps_ch11.intro: A newborn, resource-poor nation told two superpowers it would pick its own positions — and then did.
c12_ps_ch11.goal: Analyse the objectives, instruments and limits of Nehru's non-aligned foreign policy, 1946–1964.

discovery.question: In Haryana in 1967, one MLA switched parties three times in a fortnight — once within nine hours — and a Congress boss publicly joked about it. What did that farce reveal about the election's real aftershock?
options: Coalitions built only on anti-Congress unity had no programme to hold them together, and parties openly traded MLAs to make governments
Defection was illegal but impossible to prove
The MLA was unusually corrupt, nothing more
The Election Commission had collapsed
discovery.answer: Coalitions built only on anti-Congress unity had no programme to hold them together, and parties openly traded MLAs to make governments
discovery.hook: 1967 didn't split Congress — that came in 1969 over a presidential nominee. The election's real work was exposing that drought, devaluation and death had drained the party's performance legitimacy, letting Lohia's 'non-Congressism' unite rivals who agreed on nothing else.

c12_ps_ch12.mission: Run the numbers on 1967 — seven states lost, half the cabinet defeated — and trace how hunger, opposition arithmetic and defections cracked the Congress system.
c12_ps_ch12.finale: You can now see 1967 as the moment dominance became contestable: the Congress era didn't end, but its inevitability did.
c12_ps_ch12.subtitle: The year India's one-party habit broke
c12_ps_ch12.intro: A generation raised on Congress victories woke up to headlines of seven lost states and MLAs for hire.
c12_ps_ch12.goal: Analyse the 1967 verdict — non-Congressism, SVD coalitions and defection politics — as the turning point of the party system.

discovery.question: The Narmada Bachao Andolan argued cases in the Supreme Court, lobbied the World Bank and faced down state governments for decades — yet refused to join or float a political party. Apolitical?
options: Deeply political — it contested power and policy through courts, media and mobilisation, just refused party affiliation to keep the freedom to pressure every party
Apolitical — real politics only happens inside parties
Anti-political — it rejected the state entirely
It would have joined a party if offered enough seats
discovery.answer: Deeply political — it contested power and policy through courts, media and mobilisation, just refused party affiliation to keep the freedom to pressure every party
discovery.hook: Non-party doesn't mean non-political — these movements rose because the party system ignored tribals, farmers, women and forests, and staying outside parties is precisely what lets them confront all parties.

c12_ps_ch13.mission: Sort India's great movements — JP's party-backed crusade versus Chipko and NBA's party-free persistence — by who leads them, who funds them and who they answer to.
c12_ps_ch13.finale: You can now tell a party's protest from a people's movement — and argue why the second kind is a correction to democracy, not a threat to it.
c12_ps_ch13.subtitle: Politics without a party flag
c12_ps_ch13.intro: When parties stop listening, citizens don't stop organising — they just organise differently.
c12_ps_ch13.goal: Distinguish party-based from non-party movements by leadership, funding and accountability, and explain their democratic role.

discovery.question: Europe built nations by hammering diversity into one language and culture; India let parties win elections by demanding 'our water, our jobs, our language'. Why would a democracy encourage that?
options: Because regional identity is how Indian democracy negotiates unity — channelling aspirations into elections and accords flexes the federation instead of breaking it
Because India failed to build a real nation
Because regional parties are too weak to matter
Because the Constitution forbids suppressing any demand
discovery.answer: Because regional identity is how Indian democracy negotiates unity — channelling aspirations into elections and accords flexes the federation instead of breaking it
discovery.hook: Regional aspiration is not secessionism — most movements want autonomy or statehood inside India, and the typical response is a negotiated accord (Mizoram 1986, Punjab 1985), with force the exception that usually backfires.

c12_ps_ch14.mission: Map India's regional demands — autonomy, statehood, secession — to the constitutional tools built to absorb them, and weigh why Mizoram got an accord while Nagaland still waits.
c12_ps_ch14.finale: You can now argue that regionalism is a feature of Indian democracy, not a bug — and that even after Article 370, asymmetric federalism remains the architecture.
c12_ps_ch14.subtitle: Demanding your region's share is how India stays one
c12_ps_ch14.intro: A leader demanding his state's water isn't being anti-national — he's using the exact channel the system was designed to offer.
c12_ps_ch14.goal: Distinguish autonomy, statehood and secessionist demands, and evaluate India's accommodation-first approach to regional aspirations.

discovery.question: In 1989, Congress stayed the single largest party with 197 seats — and voluntarily sat in the opposition benches while its enemies' enemies teamed up to rule. Why hand over power?
options: It couldn't reach a majority and had no willing allies — so a National Front minority government ran the country on outside support from the BJP and the Left simultaneously
The President refused to invite Congress
Congress had legally lost the right to form government
It planned to merge with the Janata Dal
discovery.answer: It couldn't reach a majority and had no willing allies — so a National Front minority government ran the country on outside support from the BJP and the Left simultaneously
discovery.hook: The 'Congress system' didn't end because Congress vanished — it remained the largest party for years. What ended was its monopoly on aggregating interests: regional and ideological parties became power centres, making coalitions the new normal.

c12_ps_ch15.mission: Reconstruct the 1989 verdict and its strange bedfellows — a right-wing and a left-wing bloc propping up the same government — and test whether coalition politics weakened or deepened Indian democracy.
c12_ps_ch15.finale: You can now explain why 1989, not 1977 or 2014, marks the true end of one-party dominance — power-sharing replaced dominance for the next quarter-century.
c12_ps_ch15.subtitle: When the largest party chose the opposition benches
c12_ps_ch15.intro: One election flipped the logic of Indian power: from one party absorbing everyone, to everyone assembling against one party.
c12_ps_ch15.goal: Explain the 1989 turning point and the structural features of India's coalition era.

discovery.question: You live inside Indian society every day — so what could a subject called 'sociology of India' possibly teach you that you don't already know?
options: That your everyday knowledge is 'partial' twice over — incomplete and tilted to your own group's viewpoint — and sociology's first job is unlearning it
Nothing — common sense is enough
Only facts about villages and castes you haven't visited
Statistics you could look up anyway
discovery.answer: That your everyday knowledge is 'partial' twice over — incomplete and tilted to your own group's viewpoint — and sociology's first job is unlearning it
discovery.hook: Unlearning doesn't mean common sense is false — it means it's a view from somewhere. 'Caste doesn't matter in cities' is true from an upper-caste city address; sociology studies why both that claim and a Dalit student's opposite experience get produced.

c12_soc_ch01.mission: Locate yourself on the social map, take one personal worry — like not getting a college seat — and trace it upward into structural machinery: seats, coaching economies, reservations, regional gaps.
c12_soc_ch01.finale: You can now turn a private trouble into a public issue — the single move that makes sociology a method, not a pile of facts.
c12_soc_ch01.subtitle: The science of what you think you already know
c12_soc_ch01.intro: The hardest thing to study is the world you grew up inside — because it trained you not to notice it.
c12_soc_ch01.goal: Explain why common sense is inadequate for studying society and apply self-reflexivity and the sociological imagination.

discovery.question: Suicide looks like the most private act imaginable — yet Durkheim found its rate stays eerily stable for whole countries and varies by religion and marital status. If it's personal, why does it behave like a statistic?
options: Because the rate is a social fact — a collective pattern shaped by social causes that no individual psychology can explain
Because depressed people copy each other
Because some countries underreport it
Because climate affects mood uniformly
discovery.answer: Because the rate is a social fact — a collective pattern shaped by social causes that no individual psychology can explain
discovery.hook: Demography isn't the census — the count is just a tool. The discipline lives in rates, ratios and the social machinery behind them: why Kerala's fertility fell and Bihar's didn't is a question no headcount can answer.

c12_soc_ch02.mission: Split a population question in two — let formal demography forecast the numbers while social demography digs out the norms and power relations driving them.
c12_soc_ch02.finale: You can now tell the 'how many' from the 'why' — and see why sociology owes its scientific credibility to population statistics.
c12_soc_ch02.subtitle: Counting people was the easy part
c12_soc_ch02.intro: A census gives you 1.2 billion people. A demographer's real questions start the moment the counting stops.
c12_soc_ch02.goal: Distinguish formal from social demography and explain why population data are social facts essential to theory and policy.

discovery.question: Strip away purity and pollution but keep fixed marriages and inherited occupations — do you still have caste, or something else entirely?
options: Not caste — without purity-pollution there's no moral ladder, just separate guild-like groups; ranking by ritual distance is what makes the system one
Yes — caste is only about who marries whom
Yes — hereditary jobs alone define it
No — because caste is really about class
discovery.answer: Not caste — without purity-pollution there's no moral ladder, just separate guild-like groups; ranking by ritual distance is what makes the system one
discovery.hook: Varna is not the 'real' caste — it's a four-box scriptural ideal. Jati, the thousands of actual birth-groups people marry and eat by, is the lived institution; confusing the two flattens the whole system.

c12_soc_ch03.mission: Dissect the rulebook — birth, endogamy, food rules, hereditary work — and figure out how one institution can separate communities into boxes yet rank them on a single ladder.
c12_soc_ch03.finale: You can now see caste as a system where separation creates the hierarchy — and where ritual status keeps converting into land, capital and office.
c12_soc_ch03.subtitle: A ladder where every rung exists only relative to the others
c12_soc_ch03.intro: At the wedding, the priests, caterers and guests follow an invisible rulebook nobody wrote down — sociology's job is to read it.
c12_soc_ch03.goal: Explain the varna-jati distinction and the purity-pollution logic that makes caste both separating and hierarchical.

discovery.question: At a Bastar weekly haat, the same patch of ground hosts forest produce sales, wage payments, marriage negotiations and kin reunions — all at once. Is this an economy, or a society wearing an economy's clothes?
options: Both at once — the haat's exchange rules, credit and trader dominance run on caste, kinship and colonial history; no 'invisible hand' built this
Just an economy — buying and selling is all that matters
A society pretending to trade — the goods are incidental
A pre-market ritual that economics hasn't reached yet
discovery.answer: Both at once — the haat's exchange rules, credit and trader dominance run on caste, kinship and colonial history; no 'invisible hand' built this
discovery.hook: Don't read 'market as social institution' as 'people socialise while shopping' — the claim is stronger: caste networks like the Nakarattar bankers ran credit on community reputation alone, so markets are constituted by social relations, not merely surrounded by them.

c12_soc_ch04.mission: Read a market like a sociologist — find the caste ties, kin networks and power asymmetries holding the transactions up, then catch commodification turning hospitality into a rated service.
c12_soc_ch04.finale: You can now explain why liberalisation raised efficiency yet left the power map intact — markets don't escape society; they're built out of it.
c12_soc_ch04.subtitle: The invisible hand has a caste, a clan and a postcode
c12_soc_ch04.intro: Every price tag is the end of a chain of trust — find out who the chain trusts, and you've found the real market.
c12_soc_ch04.goal: Explain embeddedness and commodification and analyse how social relations structure Indian markets.

discovery.question: A wealthy Dalit businessman can buy the car, the house and the club membership — yet still be refused entry to a temple and a marriage alliance. If money fixed inequality, what just failed?
options: Economic capital is only one of three capitals — cultural and social capital move through networks his money can't force open
Nothing — wealth always buys status
The temple was breaking the law, that's all
He needed to work harder
discovery.answer: Economic capital is only one of three capitals — cultural and social capital move through networks his money can't force open
discovery.hook: Social inequality isn't income inequality — it's group-patterned, inherited across generations and defended by ideologies that call it fair. Cash transfers can lift poverty without touching the hierarchy that produced it.

c12_soc_ch05.mission: Audit two children's life chances using three forms of capital, then test whether the difference you find is individual bad luck or a machine built to repeat itself.
c12_soc_ch05.finale: You can now separate inequality (the gap) from stratification (the machinery that keeps the gap) — and spot the meritocracy story hiding inside it.
c12_soc_ch05.subtitle: Why the gap keeps reproducing itself
c12_soc_ch05.intro: Two kids, one neighbourhood, different planets — sociology asks who built the planets.
c12_soc_ch05.goal: Distinguish social inequality from individual differences and from stratification, using Bourdieu's three capitals.

discovery.question: In 1956 Sri Lanka declared one national language and slid toward civil war; that same decade India carved its states by language and got 'perfectly consistent to be Kannadiga and Indian'. Same impulse, opposite result — why?
options: Sri Lanka's assimilation told minorities their identity didn't count; India's accommodation let regional identities coexist inside national unity
India just got lucky
Sri Lanka had more diversity to manage
Indian languages were easier to reorganise
discovery.answer: Sri Lanka's assimilation told minorities their identity didn't count; India's accommodation let regional identities coexist inside national unity
discovery.hook: Community identity isn't like a professional membership you can resign — it's ascriptive, born into you, which is why threats to language or faith ignite so fast. Diversity becomes a 'problem' only when a state treats difference as disloyalty.

c12_soc_ch06.mission: Contrast assimilationist and integrationist nation-states with India's state-nation model, and test whether accommodating 1,600-odd languages strengthened or strained the union.
c12_soc_ch06.finale: You can now argue with data that recognising diversity built Indian unity — while insisting on sameness broke neighbours apart.
c12_soc_ch06.subtitle: Unity in diversity is a policy, not a poster
c12_soc_ch06.intro: One metro coach, five languages, four faiths — the puzzle isn't how India differs, it's how it holds.
c12_soc_ch06.goal: Define cultural diversity, distinguish nation from nation-state, and evaluate India's state-nation model.

discovery.question: You've read a full chapter on how households divide labour by gender — now you're told to actually investigate three real households. Why does the textbook insist the fieldwork matters more than the findings?
options: Because doing research teaches what reading can't — formulating a question, picking a fitting method, and surviving non-response, access problems and ethical mess
Because your findings might get published
Because fieldwork is cheaper than teaching theory
Because surveys always beat textbooks
discovery.answer: Because doing research teaches what reading can't — formulating a question, picking a fitting method, and surviving non-response, access problems and ethical mess
discovery.hook: Project work isn't 'collect data and count it' — a polished questionnaire you can't justify is data collection, not research. The question chooses the method: meanings need interviews, behaviours need observation, patterns need surveys.

c12_soc_ch07.mission: Take one broad topic, sharpen it into a researchable question, and defend a single method against the two criteria that actually decide it — technical fit and practical feasibility.
c12_soc_ch07.finale: You can now explain why 'surveys reach more people' is not an argument — the right method is the one your question demands and your field allows.
c12_soc_ch07.subtitle: You can't learn to swim from a manual
c12_soc_ch07.intro: The gap between the textbook and the neighbourhood is where sociology actually happens.
c12_soc_ch07.goal: Explain the rationale for project work and how research questions determine method selection.

discovery.question: The British built schools to mass-produce loyal clerks — and out walked a generation that used English arguments about liberty to demand the British leave. What went wrong for the empire?
options: Colonial rule contradicted its own ideals: education exposed Indians to sovereignty and equality that foreign rule denied, so nationalism armed itself with the coloniser's tools
Indians mistranslated the textbooks
The British accidentally funded the freedom movement
Nationalism arrived fully formed from outside
discovery.answer: Colonial rule contradicted its own ideals: education exposed Indians to sovereignty and equality that foreign rule denied, so nationalism armed itself with the coloniser's tools
discovery.hook: Colonialism wasn't just tribute like earlier conquests — it rewired the economic base: land became property, crops became exports, forests became timber, people became shipped labour. The railways ran port-ward, not for you.

c12_soc_ch08.mission: Follow the profit motive through land laws, cash crops, forest acts and indentured ships — and spot the paradoxes the empire couldn't see coming.
c12_soc_ch08.finale: You can now argue why the railways 'modernised' India in exactly the direction Britain's economy needed — and why Indian democracy grew against colonialism, not from it.
c12_soc_ch08.subtitle: The empire that trained its own gravediggers
c12_soc_ch08.intro: We drive on the left, learn in English and fight for freedom with the coloniser's vocabulary — colonialism's contradictions are still in the room.
c12_soc_ch08.goal: Explain how capitalist colonialism restructured India's economy and society, and analyse its paradoxical legacies.

discovery.question: A Dalit officer clears the civil services on merit, works in a rule-bound bureaucracy — then marries within his sub-caste after a priest matches horoscopes. Modernised or not?
options: Partially — modernisation is domain-specific: the same person can run on achieved identity at work and ascribed identity at home
Fully — an elite job makes you modern
Not at all — arranged marriage cancels it
He's westernised, not modernised
discovery.answer: Partially — modernisation is domain-specific: the same person can run on achieved identity at work and ascribed identity at home
discovery.hook: Jeans, English and a Christmas tree are westernisation — borrowed forms. Modernisation is deeper: rationality, universalism, the individual over the group. A household can have air-conditioning and dowry in the same room — forms without values.

c12_soc_ch09.mission: Sort real lives — the tractor village, the IT professional, the khap WhatsApp group — into modernisation, westernisation and tradition armed with new tech.
c12_soc_ch09.finale: You can now separate structural change from costume change — and explain why India modernised without becoming a copy of the West.
c12_soc_ch09.subtitle: New phone, old rules — which change actually counts?
c12_soc_ch09.intro: Technology moves faster than values — sociology's job is telling the two apart.
c12_soc_ch09.goal: Distinguish modernisation from westernisation and analyse India's domain-specific, colonial-shaped path to modernity.

discovery.question: A country holds regular elections with universal suffrage — but the ruling party owns the media, the courts and the election commission, and rivals keep getting arrested. Democracy or not?
options: Only procedurally — it has the voting machinery but fails accountability and rule of law, the substantive core that makes power genuinely answerable
Yes — elections alone define democracy
No — it's a plain dictatorship
Yes — until proven otherwise in court
discovery.answer: Only procedurally — it has the voting machinery but fails accountability and rule of law, the substantive core that makes power genuinely answerable
discovery.hook: Democracy isn't binary — a village gram sabha and the Lok Sabha both count, differently. And reserved seats for women are a procedural guarantee; where 'sarpanch-patis' pull the strings, substance hasn't arrived.

c12_soc_ch10.mission: Classify regimes along the procedural-subjective axis — then defend India's parliamentary, representative design against the direct and presidential alternatives.
c12_soc_ch10.finale: You can now argue that democracy is a continuous negotiation between state and society — which is why one constitutional amendment can empower a village while another can merely decorate it.
c12_soc_ch10.subtitle: Elections are the floor, not the ceiling
c12_soc_ch10.intro: 'We, the people' is a claim that has to be re-proven between elections — courts, media and street all get a say.
c12_soc_ch10.goal: Distinguish procedural from substantive democracy and classify democratic forms by constitutional design.

discovery.question: In one Bengal village a zamindar skimmed rent from fifty families to pay the British; in a Madras village the ryot paid the taxman directly — and still went hungry to the moneylender. Two systems, same result. What was the machine underneath?
options: Colonial revenue design — both froze a hierarchy where dominant castes held land and landless labour was hereditary; the intermediary changed, the extraction didn't
The zamindari system was uniquely cruel
Raiyatwari made every cultivator an owner
The difference was only paperwork
discovery.answer: Colonial revenue design — both froze a hierarchy where dominant castes held land and landless labour was hereditary; the intermediary changed, the extraction didn't
discovery.hook: Raiyatwari didn't abolish landlords — registered ryots sublet, and moneylenders turned debt into land. And a tenant is not a labourer: one held cultivation rights, however shaky; the other owned only their labour.

c12_soc_ch11.mission: Trace the paddy from field to collector under zamindari and raiyatwari — counting who keeps what at each stage and where caste enters the arithmetic.
c12_soc_ch11.finale: You can now see why land control and caste power fused under colonialism — the inequality land reform later had to dig out.
c12_soc_ch11.subtitle: Two tax systems, one hierarchy
c12_soc_ch11.intro: In 1890, who paid the tax told you who owned the village — and usually which caste they were born into.
c12_soc_ch11.goal: Distinguish zamindari from raiyatwari systems and explain the caste-class structure of colonial agrarian society.

discovery.question: A Bengal weaver picks the pattern, sets the pace, owns the loom and the cloth. A Tirupur machinist stitches one seam, shift-timed, for a wage, and never sees the finished shirt. Same industry — what actually changed?
options: Control over the labour process itself — the artisan owns tools and product; the worker sells labour-power and answers to the machine's pace
Nothing but the technology
Only the wages
The factory worker is more skilled
discovery.answer: Control over the labour process itself — the artisan owns tools and product; the worker sells labour-power and answers to the machine's pace
discovery.hook: India never replayed the European script — colonial rule destroyed handicrafts without building factories to absorb the artisans, and nine in ten Indian workers still labour informally. Bidi rollers at home are industrial workers who never see a factory.

c12_soc_ch12.mission: Contrast the handloom with the assembly line across control, product and hierarchy — then map why India's version runs on contract labour and home-based piece rates.
c12_soc_ch12.finale: You can now explain industrialisation as a rewiring of social relations, not just machines — and why liberalisation grew jobs while shrinking job security.
c12_soc_ch12.subtitle: The machine didn't just make cloth — it remade the worker
c12_soc_ch12.intro: The saree and the polyester shirt carry different histories: one of a maker, one of a pair of hands.
c12_soc_ch12.goal: Analyse the handicraft-to-factory shift as social change and identify India's distinct informal-sector trajectory.

discovery.question: Your morning: alarm on a Chinese phone, shirt stitched in Bangladesh, coffee from Brazil, a tutor in Bengaluru on a US-hosted app — all before 8 AM, while your farmer uncle watches imported oilseeds crash his prices. One process or many?
options: One process — globalisation stretching social and economic relationships worldwide, driven by the ICT revolution inside a neo-liberal policy frame, creating winners and losers in the same family
Just more Silk Route — trade is as old as history
Only economics — culture and politics aren't involved
Westernisation — the West remaking everyone else
discovery.answer: One process — globalisation stretching social and economic relationships worldwide, driven by the ICT revolution inside a neo-liberal policy frame, creating winners and losers in the same family
discovery.hook: Globalisation isn't just Americanisation — Korean silk displaces Bihar spinners, Sudanese gum displaces Gujarat collectors. And McDonald's going vegetarian for Navaratri isn't fusion for culture's sake; it's a market strategy that keeps the global brand in charge.

c12_soc_ch13.mission: Dissect one ordinary day into globalisation's economic, political and cultural threads — then trace why it lifts a Noida BPO worker while ending a Varanasi weaver's orders.
c12_soc_ch13.finale: You can now hold both truths at once — new opportunity and lost livelihood — which is exactly what 'uneven impact' means.
c12_soc_ch13.subtitle: The world in your pocket, the squeeze in the village
c12_soc_ch13.intro: Five border-crossings before breakfast — the question is who arranged them, and who pays for them.
c12_soc_ch13.goal: Define globalisation's dimensions and drivers, and analyse its uneven impact and glocalisation in India.

discovery.question: A Bihar village rigs an FM transmitter on a bamboo pole and broadcasts folk songs and health messages to 20 km — no company, no budget, no licence. Mass media or not?
options: Yes — mass media is defined by one-to-many reach to a large anonymous audience, not by corporate scale
No — real mass media needs a big organisation
No — it's just loudspeakers with extra steps
Yes — but only because it's radio
discovery.answer: Yes — mass media is defined by one-to-many reach to a large anonymous audience, not by corporate scale
discovery.hook: Media isn't a neutral mirror — the big organisations behind it have owners, mandates and gatekeepers who select and frame what you see. And the digital divide isn't about who owns a phone; it's about literacy, language, data costs and who in the house is allowed to hold it.

c12_soc_ch14.mission: Track how All India Radio sold the Green Revolution while farmers reshaped its programmes — then test what mass media's institutional machinery does to the 'news' you trust.
c12_soc_ch14.finale: You can now separate the institution from the process, and see media as a two-way street: it reflects society while quietly rebuilding it.
c12_soc_ch14.subtitle: Whoever owns the tower shapes the story
c12_soc_ch14.intro: Every message that reaches millions passed through a structure with interests of its own.
c12_soc_ch14.goal: Define mass media's structural features and analyse the dialectical relationship between media and society.

discovery.question: In 1838, over a million workers signed a charter demanding the vote — meeting, organising, campaigning for years. A century later a hungry crowd can riot over bread prices and disperse by evening. Both are 'people acting together' — so what makes only one a movement?
options: Sustained organisation, shared ideology and a goal beyond the moment — a riot has a grievance; a movement has a charter, leaders and a strategy
Size — a million signatures beats a street crowd
Violence — riots don't count as movements
Age — movements must be historical
discovery.answer: Sustained organisation, shared ideology and a goal beyond the moment — a riot has a grievance; a movement has a charter, leaders and a strategy
discovery.hook: Big crowds don't make movements — 1857 lacked unified organisation and shared ideology across centres, so it's a rebellion, not a movement. And Chipko wasn't 'just environmental': its villagers fused survival economics, ecology and anger at a distant state into one fight.

c12_soc_ch15.mission: Run real cases through the movement checklist — sanskritisation, a station protest, the anti-sati campaign, Chipko — and defend what qualifies and what's merely collective heat.
c12_soc_ch15.finale: You can now tell social change (a tide), collective behaviour (a spark) and a social movement (an engine) apart — and explain why your weekends exist because someone organised.
c12_soc_ch15.subtitle: A riot burns out; a movement keeps minutes
c12_soc_ch15.intro: The eight-hour day and the vote weren't granted — they were organised for, signature by signature.
c12_soc_ch15.goal: Distinguish social movements from collective behaviour and social change using organisation, ideology and sustained action.
